**I.**


1. A company has three factories producing a product. Factory 1 produces x1 of
the product, factory 2 produces x2, and factory 3 produces x3, where the sum
of these is 1. The defective rates of the products are y1, y2, and y3
respectively, where the sum of these is 0.12. Write a program (user input for
xi and yi) to calculate the probability that a randomly selected product is
defective.


![Input x1, x2, and x3]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 1.1.jpg")


![Input y1, y2, and y3]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 1.2.jpg")


The user input 0.3, 0.35, and 0.35 for the production of the 3 factories. All
of these ranged between 0.1 and 0.4 and equals to 1 when added. Their
defective rates are: 0.0356, 0.0409, and 0.0435, respectively. These rates are
in between of 0.01 and 0.05 and totalled to 0.12. The probability of picking
a defective product is 0.04022 or 4.022%.




2. With your own computing experience, develop a front end to R that allows
the user to input the values of a univariate discrete random variable and the
associated probabilities and to obtain the mean and variance, and to input
the values of a bivariate discrete random variable and the associated
probabilities and to obtain the marginal and conditional distributions. Your
program should provide a facility to calculate the mean and variance of each
distribution, and to plot the pdf and cdf. In each program, do validity checks
that the probabilities are in the interval [0, 1], and that they sum to one.


UNIVARIATE DISTRIBUTION


![Univariate Distribution]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 2.1.jpg")


![Univariate Distribution - PDF & CDF]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 2.1 plot.jpg")


Reusing the percentage of each selecting products from each factory from the
previous item, the graphs show their probability, with the two 0.35 having a
higher chance compared to the 0.30. Meanwhile, the other graph depicts the
totality that adds up from the lowest value (0.3) until the maximium value.



BIVARIATE DISTRIBUTION


![Bivariate Distribution]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 2.2.1.jpg")


![Bivariate Distribution]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 2.2.2.jpg")


![Bivariate Distribution - X0]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 2.2 plot x0.jpg")


![Bivariate Distribution - X1]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 2.2 plot x1.jpg")


![Bivariate Distribution - Y0]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 2.2 plot y0.jpg")


![Bivariate Distribution - Y1]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 2.2 plot y1.jpg")


The user intended to try the probabilities of tossing a coin 2x, with X
represents the 1st toss and the Y is the 2nd toss, and 0 and 1 as heads and
tails, respectively. Marginal distribution shows that all are possible
outcomes and has the probability of 0.25. Both 1st and 2nd toss have 0.5
chance of getting a head or a tail, and both have the same mean (0.5) and
variance (0.25). The conditional distribution tells us that the 1st toss does
not affect the 2nd toss and vice versa.




3. By generating 10,000 searches in R, carry out a simulation experiment for a
search engine going through a list of sites for a given key phrase, until the
key phrase is found. You should allow your program to input the probability p
that any site will contain the key phrase.


Plot the simulated pdf and calculate its mean and variance, and obtain the
simulated conditional distribution of searches when three searches have been
carried out without success. Calculate its mean and variance, and satisfy
yourself that they are equivalent to the simulated distribution of the
complete set. As test data assume each site has a 60% chance of containing the
key phrase. To satisfy yourself that the Markov memoryless property holds,
obtain estimates of (a) P(X=4|X>3) and P(X=1), and (b) P(X=5|X>3) and P(X=2)
where X is the number of searches to the first success.


![Simulated PDF]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 3.1.jpg")


![Simulated PDF - Graph]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 3.1 plot1.jpg")


![Conditional PDF]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 3.2.jpg")


![Conditional PDF - Graph]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 3.2 plot.jpg")


![Markov Memoryless Property]("D:\r fas\sa 1\sa1 seci 3.3.jpg")


With a success chance of 60%, is the same as the theoretical probability of
the first search being successful, while on the second search is 24%. The graph
shows that the probability of the first success decreases as the required
number of searches increases. The expected number of searches is about 1.67
and the variance is around 1.11, which are close to the simulated results. By
the Memoryless Property, the probability of success on the next try is still
0.6, disregarding the previous failed attempts, which is the same for the
next search at 0.24. This suggests that the theoretical probabilities before
and after 3 failures equal to the corresponding waiting times. But the
simulated ones are not exactly equal as this consists of finite random trials.
